warmup.q: A transition bus is MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = DROP_LATEST). A fast notifier and an audit writer that needs 1 s per row both subscribe. Six transitions are emitted 10 ms apart. What does the fast notifier receive?
options: All six: DROP_LATEST only drops values for the slow subscriber
1, 2 and 3: values 4, 5 and 6 are dropped for everyone
1 and 2: the buffer holds two values
warmup.why: Every subscriber reads from one shared buffer. The audit writer took 1 and is busy, so 2 and 3 fill the two slots it still needs. When 4 arrives the buffer is full, and DROP_LATEST throws 4 away before anyone can read it, notifier included. The same happens to 5 and 6.

sections.h: One slow subscriber decides what the fast one gets
sections.html:
A teammate wired up this transition bus. The notifier sends receipts and is fast. The audit writer needs a full second per row, so they picked DROP_LATEST: when the audit writer falls behind, it should drop transitions while the notifier carries on.

Java
// Java equivalent: a Reactor multicast sink; the audit subscriber requests one item, then stalls
Sinks.Many<Integer> bus = Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing();
bus.asFlux().subscribe(notifier::add);          // fast: unbounded demand
bus.asFlux().subscribe(auditThatRequestsOne);   // slow: request(1), then nothing
for (int t = 1; t <= 6; t++) bus.tryEmitNext(t);
Kotlin
val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST)
backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { notifier += it } }              // fast
backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { audit += it; delay(1_000) } }   // 1 s per row
for (transition in 1..6) { bus.emit(transition); delay(10) }

Predict what the notifier receives. Here is the output in virtual time, with the other two policies for comparison:

DROP_LATEST   notifier got [1, 2, 3]            audit got [1, 2, 3]
SUSPEND       notifier got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   audit got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   emit(4), (5), (6) returned at t=1000, 2000, 3000
DROP_OLDEST   notifier got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   audit got [1, 5, 6]

The notifier lost 4, 5 and 6, and it was never slow. To see why, picture a MutableSharedFlow as a radio station that records onto one tape loop. The emitter is the DJ, and every subscriber is a playback head on that same tape. There is no queue per subscriber. Old tape can only be cleared behind the slowest head, so the slowest subscriber decides when the tape is full, for everyone.

Walk through it. The audit writer takes 1 and starts its one-second write. Values 2 and 3 go onto the tape, which has room for exactly two (extraBufferCapacity). The notifier reads them at once, but that clears nothing, because the audit head still needs them. Value 4 finds the tape full, and the policy decides what happens:

  • SUSPEND, the default: emit(4) waits until the audit writer takes 2, at t=1000. The notifier has nothing new to read, so it waits as well.
  • DROP_LATEST: 4 is never recorded. Nobody hears it.
  • DROP_OLDEST: 4 is recorded over 2, and the audit head is pushed past the part that was overwritten. Only the slow subscriber skips.

That makes the overflow policy a choice about every subscriber at once. When no transition may be lost and the notifier must not wait, keep SUSPEND and give the slow subscriber a buffer of its own. bus.buffer(64).collect { ... } puts a channel between the tape and the slow work (lesson 4 of this track), so the audit head takes values off the tape at once. In the Try it, that version delivers all six to both, and every emit returns by t=50. The cushion has a size: once those 64 slots fill, the audit side stops taking from the tape, and everyone waits again.

Six transitions are emitted 10 ms apart. // All times are virtual milliseconds (runTest), so the output is the same on every run. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun busWith(policy: BufferOverflow, auditHasOwnBuffer: Boolean = false) = runTest { val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = policy) val notifier = mutableListOf<Int>() val audit = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { notifier += it } } val auditSide = if (auditHasOwnBuffer) bus.buffer(64) else bus // a channel of its own in front of the slow work backgroundScope.launch { auditSide.collect { audit += it; delay(1_000) } } runCurrent() // both have subscribed and wait for a value val returned = mutableListOf<String>() for (transition in 1..6) { bus.emit(transition) returned += "$transition@t=$currentTime" delay(10) } advanceTimeBy(10_000); runCurrent() println(if (auditHasOwnBuffer) "$policy, audit collects bus.buffer(64)" else "$policy") println(" notifier got $notifier") println(" audit got $audit") println(" emit returned: $returned") } fun main() { busWith(BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) busWith(BufferOverflow.SUSPEND) busWith(BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) busWith(BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, auditHasOwnBuffer = true) }

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l07; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; // Java equivalent: Reactor multicast sinks with one fast subscriber and one slow one. // The slow audit writer asks for one transition and then nothing more until the end, // as if stuck on its first row. Everything runs on the main thread, so no timing is involved. public class FastAndSlowJava { static final class SlowAudit extends BaseSubscriber<Integer> { final List<Integer> got = new ArrayList<>(); @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer v) { got.add(v); } } static void run(String label, Sinks.Many<Integer> bus, boolean auditHasOwnBuffer) { List<Integer> notifier = new ArrayList<>(); bus.asFlux().subscribe(notifier::add); // unbounded demand SlowAudit audit = new SlowAudit(); // demand of 1, or a buffer of its own in front of the slow work (auditHasOwnBuffer ? bus.asFlux().onBackpressureBuffer(64) : bus.asFlux()).subscribe(audit); List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 1; t <= 6; t++) results.add(t + "=" + bus.tryEmitNext(t)); String notifierBefore = notifier.toString(); audit.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); // the audit writer catches up at the end System.out.println(label); System.out.println(" tryEmitNext: " + results); System.out.println(" notifier had " + notifierBefore + " while the audit writer was stuck"); System.out.println(" notifier got " + notifier); System.out.println(" audit got " + audit.got); } public static void main(String[] args) { run("multicast().directAllOrNothing()", Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(), false); run("multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(1, false)", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(1, false), false); // one slot run("multicast().directBestEffort()", Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(), false); run("onBackpressureBuffer(1, false), audit subscribes through onBackpressureBuffer(64)", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(1, false), true); } }

try.expect: DROP_LATEST: both get [1, 2, 3], and every emit returns at once. SUSPEND: both get all six, but emit(4), emit(5) and emit(6) return at t=1000, 2000 and 3000, so the fast notifier waits for the audit writer. DROP_OLDEST: the notifier gets all six and the audit writer [1, 5, 6]. With bus.buffer(64) on the audit side, both get all six and every emit returns by t=50. With a buffer of 3, DROP_LATEST gives both [1, 2, 3, 4], and under SUSPEND the first to wait is emit(5), which returns at t=1000. The Java twin shows the same choices with Reactor sinks: directAllOrNothing() refuses 2 to 6 for both subscribers (FAIL_OVERFLOW), a one-slot onBackpressureBuffer holds the notifier at [1] while the audit writer is stuck, directBestEffort() drops only for the stalled subscriber (a setting Kotlin's SharedFlow doesn't have), and onBackpressureBuffer(64) on the audit side frees the notifier.

sections.h: The exact rule: count what the slowest subscriber hasn't taken
sections.html:
emit is two steps in the source: if (tryEmit(value)) return, and only then suspend. So one rule answers both questions, when emit waits and when tryEmit returns false.

  1. With no subscribers, every call succeeds. The value goes into the replay cache if replay > 0, and nowhere otherwise. extraBufferCapacity plays no part: with replay = 2, extraBufferCapacity = 10, five emits to nobody leave replayCache = [4, 5].
  2. With subscribers, the tape holds replay + extraBufferCapacity values, and it is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it has not taken yet. Then SUSPEND makes tryEmit return false and emit wait, while the two drop policies return true and drop.

"Taken" has an exact meaning. A subscriber takes a value when it reads it off the tape, before your collect lambda runs. A value that a busy subscriber is still working on no longer counts. That is why the audit writer in the first section held only 2 and 3 against the tape, and not 1.

Now the default, MutableSharedFlow(), with no replay and no extra buffer. There is no tape at all, so a value can only pass like a relay baton. The runner (emit) holds it out and lets go once every receiver has a hand on it. tryEmit throws the baton without waiting, and it falls. tryEmit therefore returns false whenever there is a subscriber, even an idle one, as lesson 8 of the coroutines track said. And emit returns the moment the subscriber takes the value, before the subscriber has done anything with it: with 100 ms of work per value, emit(1), emit(2) and emit(3) return at t=0, 100 and 200.

Here is the rule at work. One subscriber has subscribed and waits, then tryEmit(1) to tryEmit(6) run back to back (T is true, f is false):

Flow tryEmit(1..6) The subscriber gets
MutableSharedFlow(), no subscriber T T T T T T (nobody there)
MutableSharedFlow() f f f f f f nothing
extraBufferCapacity = 2 T T f f f f 1, 2
replay = 2 T T f f f f 1, 2
replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2 T T T f f f 1, 2, 3
extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST T T T T T T 5, 6
extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_LATEST T T T T T T 1, 2

Two rows deserve a second look. While someone is subscribed, replay = 2 behaves exactly like extraBufferCapacity = 2: both are slots on the one tape. And three idle subscribers give the same row as one, because they share the tape.

The tape also explains a subscriber that arrives late. It is like walking into a cinema mid-film: you get the recap (the replay cache), then the live film. You never see the scenes the slow viewer in row 3 is still catching up on. With replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 10, a subscriber stuck on value 1 while 1 to 5 are emitted works through all five, and a second subscriber that joins after 5 gets only [5].

code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest // When does tryEmit return false? One subscriber subscribes and waits, then tryEmit(1..6) // runs back to back, so the subscriber can't take anything between two calls. Virtual time. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun table(label: String, flow: MutableSharedFlow<Int>, subscribers: Int = 1) = runTest { val got = mutableListOf<Int>() repeat(subscribers) { s -> backgroundScope.launch { flow.collect { if (s == 0) got += it; delay(100) } } } runCurrent() val results = (1..6).map { flow.tryEmit(it) }.joinToString(" ") { if (it) "T" else "f" } advanceTimeBy(10_000); runCurrent() // advanceUntilIdle() would not run backgroundScope println("%-30s subscribers=%d tryEmit: %s received: %s".format(label, subscribers, results, got)) } // The rendezvous: with no buffer, emit waits until the subscriber has TAKEN the value. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun rendezvous() = runTest { val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { println(" t=$currentTime subscriber took $it"); delay(100) } } runCurrent() for (v in 1..3) { bus.emit(v); println(" t=$currentTime emit($v) returned") } } // A late subscriber gets the replay cache, then live values. Never the slow one's backlog. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun late() = runTest { val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 10) val s1 = mutableListOf<Int>(); val s2 = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { s1 += it; delay(100) } } runCurrent() (1..5).forEach { bus.emit(it) } // S1 is still busy with 1 backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { s2 += it } } advanceTimeBy(1_000); runCurrent() println(" S1 (there from the start) got $s1, S2 (joined after 5) got $s2") } fun main() { println("== tryEmit(1..6) with a waiting subscriber") table("MutableSharedFlow()", MutableSharedFlow(), subscribers = 0) table("MutableSharedFlow()", MutableSharedFlow()) table("MutableSharedFlow()", MutableSharedFlow(), subscribers = 3) table("extraBufferCapacity=2", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2)) table("replay=2", MutableSharedFlow(replay = 2)) table("replay=1, extra=2", MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2)) table("extra=2, DROP_OLDEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)) table("extra=2, DROP_LATEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST)) println("== emit on MutableSharedFlow(), subscriber needs 100 ms per value") rendezvous() println("== a late subscriber, replay=1, extra=10") late() }

A subscriber says "I can take n" // with request(n) BEFORE anything is emitted, so a sink can push straight into it. public class OneTapeJava { static final class Waiting extends BaseSubscriber<Integer> { final List<Integer> got = new ArrayList<>(); @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } // idle, ready for one @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer v) { got.add(v); } } static void table(String label, Sinks.Many<Integer> sink, int subscribers) { Waiting first = null; for (int i = 0; i < subscribers; i++) { Waiting w = new Waiting(); sink.asFlux().subscribe(w); if (first == null) first = w; } List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int v = 1; v <= 6; v++) results.add(sink.tryEmitNext(v).toString()); if (first != null) first.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); System.out.printf("%-36s subscribers=%d %s received: %s%n", label, subscribers, results, first == null ? "[]" : first.got); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== tryEmitNext(1..6), each subscriber has requested 1"); table("multicast().directAllOrNothing()", Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(), 0); table("multicast().directAllOrNothing()", Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(), 1); table("multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2)", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2, false), 1); table("replay().limit(2)", Sinks.many().replay().limit(2), 1); System.out.println("== a late subscriber to replay().limit(1)"); Sinks.Many<Integer> bus = Sinks.many().replay().limit(1); Waiting s1 = new Waiting(); bus.asFlux().subscribe(s1); for (int v = 1; v <= 5; v++) bus.tryEmitNext(v); // S1 is still on its first item List<Integer> s2 = new ArrayList<>(); bus.asFlux().subscribe(s2::add); s1.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); System.out.println(" S1 got " + s1.got + ", S2 (joined after 5) got " + s2); } }

try.expect: The lines match the table, and three subscribers give the same line as one. Each emit returns at the same virtual time as subscriber took, so it waits for the take, not for the 100 ms of work. The late subscriber gets [5] while the first one works through [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. In the Java twin the first tryEmitNext to an idle subscriber returns OK and the rest FAIL_OVERFLOW: a Reactor subscriber announces its demand with request(1) before anything is emitted, so the sink can hand one item straight over. With no subscriber Reactor answers FAIL_ZERO_SUBSCRIBER, where Kotlin answers true and the value goes nowhere. A replay().limit(2) sink accepts all six, and the stalled subscriber still gets all six once it asks: the limit only decides what a late subscriber gets, and the late subscriber to limit(1) gets [5], as in Kotlin.

sections.h: StateFlow is a notice board with one slot
sections.html:
A StateFlow has no tape. It is a notice board with one slot. Two rules follow, and both compare with equals.

Pinning an equal sheet does nothing. The setter checks the new value against the current one and returns early when they are equal: no collector wakes up, and the old object stays on the board. After board.value = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.0850")) on a board that holds an equal quote, board.value === first is still true. Equality is whatever your type says, so BigDecimal("1.08500") counts as a new rate, because BigDecimal.equals compares the scale too.

Each reader remembers the last sheet they read. A collector that wakes up reads the slot, and it emits only if the value differs from the one it emitted last. A busy collector skips everything in between, including a value that went away and came back:

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor conflates and skips repeats only when you add both operators
Sinks.Many<String> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault("AUTHORIZED");
status.asFlux().onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(busyReader);
status.tryEmitNext("CAPTURED");
status.tryEmitNext("AUTHORIZED");
// busyReader got [AUTHORIZED]; without the two operators it gets all three
Kotlin
val status = MutableStateFlow("AUTHORIZED")
launch { status.collect { log += it; delay(100) } }   // 100 ms of work per value
delay(10); status.value = "CAPTURED"
delay(10); status.value = "AUTHORIZED"
// log is [AUTHORIZED]: the board changed twice, and the busy reader saw nothing new

An audit trail built on a StateFlow loses exactly these transitions. Use it for state, and a SharedFlow for events.

Writes go through compare-and-set. update { it + 1 } is a loop: read the value, compute the next one, call compareAndSet(prev, next), and go round again if another writer got in first. With 8 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default each adding 1 a hundred thousand times, the value ends at exactly 800,000, and in one run the lambda ran 1,405,098 times. Any side effect inside update { }, such as a log line, a metric or a call, runs more than once. Compute inside the lambda and act after it. compareAndSet compares with equals as well, which gives one odd case: compareAndSet(11, 11) on a board that holds 11 returns true, changes nothing and wakes nobody. Java's AtomicReference.compareAndSet compares references instead, so a fresh BigDecimal("10") fails against the stored one.

One counter does not conflate: subscriptionCount. It works like a turnstile that prints every click on a paper strip. A subscriber that walks in and straight out still leaves +1 and -1 on the strip. An observer saw [0, 1, 0] for such a visitor, where a plain StateFlow set to 1 and back to 0 showed only [0]. Sharing is built on this count.

code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger data class Quote(val pair: String, val mid: BigDecimal) // A StateFlow is a notice board with one slot. Parts A, B, C and E use virtual time. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { runTest { println("== A: equal values") val first = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.0850")) val board = MutableStateFlow(first) val seen = mutableListOf<Quote>() backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { board.collect { seen += it } } board.value = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.0850")) // equal fields println(" after an equal set: board still holds the first object? ${board.value === first}") board.value = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.08500")) // one more zero println(" collector saw ${seen.map { it.mid }}") } runTest { println("== B: AUTHORIZED -> CAPTURED -> AUTHORIZED while the collector is busy") val status = MutableStateFlow("AUTHORIZED") val log = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { status.collect { log += "t=$currentTime $it"; delay(100) } } runCurrent() delay(10); status.value = "CAPTURED" delay(10); status.value = "AUTHORIZED" advanceTimeBy(500); runCurrent() println(" busy collector saw $log") } println("== C: compareAndSet") val count = MutableStateFlow(10) println(" cas(10, 11) = ${count.compareAndSet(10, 11)}, value ${count.value}") println(" cas(10, 12) = ${count.compareAndSet(10, 12)}, value ${count.value} (stale expect)") println(" cas(11, 11) = ${count.compareAndSet(11, 11)}, value ${count.value} (true, and nobody is woken)") println("== D: update { } from 8 coroutines x 100,000 on Dispatchers.Default (REAL threads)") val calls = AtomicInteger() val counter = MutableStateFlow(0) runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(8) { launch { repeat(100_000) { counter.update { calls.incrementAndGet(); it + 1 } } } } } println(" value=${counter.value}, the lambda ran ${calls.get()} times") runTest { println("== E: subscriptionCount keeps every change") val events = MutableSharedFlow<Int>() val counts = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { events.subscriptionCount.collect { counts += it } } runCurrent() val visitor = backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { events.collect { } } visitor.cancel() // joined and left before the observer ran again runCurrent() val plain = MutableStateFlow(0); val plainSeen = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { plain.collect { plainSeen += it } } runCurrent() plain.value = 1; plain.value = 0; runCurrent() println(" subscriptionCount observer saw $counts; a plain StateFlow doing 0 -> 1 -> 0 showed $plainSeen") } }

" + new BigDecimal("1.0850").equals(new BigDecimal("1.08500")) + "; compareTo == 0? " + (new BigDecimal("1.0850").compareTo(new BigDecimal("1.08500")) == 0)); System.out.println("== B: AUTHORIZED -> CAPTURED -> AUTHORIZED while the subscriber is busy"); for (boolean asStateFlow : new boolean[] {false, true}) { Sinks.Many<String> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault("AUTHORIZED"); Busy busy = new Busy(); (asStateFlow ? status.asFlux().onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged() : status.asFlux()).subscribe(busy); status.tryEmitNext("CAPTURED"); status.tryEmitNext("AUTHORIZED"); busy.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); // no longer busy System.out.println(" " + (asStateFlow ? "with onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged(): " : "plain replay sink: ") + busy.got); } System.out.println("== C: compareAndSet on AtomicReference compares references, not equals"); AtomicReference<BigDecimal> limit = new AtomicReference<>(new BigDecimal("10")); System.out.println(" cas(new 10, 11) = " + limit.compareAndSet(new BigDecimal("10"), new BigDecimal("11")) + ", value " + limit.get()); System.out.println("== D: updateAndGet from 8 threads x 100,000 (REAL threads)"); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicReference<Integer> counter = new AtomicReference<>(0); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) counter.updateAndGet(x -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); return x + 1; }); })); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.println(" value=" + counter.get() + ", the lambda ran " + calls.get() + " times"); System.out.println("== E: currentSubscriberCount() is a number you read, with no history"); Sinks.Many<Integer> events = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(); System.out.println(" before: " + events.currentSubscriberCount()); events.asFlux().subscribe().dispose(); // a visitor joins and leaves System.out.println(" after a visitor came and went: " + events.currentSubscriberCount()); } }

try.expect: A: the board still holds the first object after the equal set, and the collector sees [1.0850, 1.08500]. B: only [t=0 AUTHORIZED]. C: true, false, true, with the value still 11. D: exactly 800000, with the lambda run far more than 800,000 times (1,405,098 in one run here). E: [0, 1, 0] against [0]. In the Java twin, BigDecimal.equals says 1.0850 and 1.08500 differ while compareTo says they are equal. The plain replay sink delivers all three statuses, and the one with onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged() delivers only [AUTHORIZED]. AtomicReference.compareAndSet fails because it compares references, and the expected BigDecimal is a different object. updateAndGet re-runs its lambda the same way. currentSubscriberCount() is a plain number, 0 before and after the visitor, with no record of the visit.

sections.h: Sharing is one pump and many taps
sections.html:
stateIn and shareIn read like conversions, and each one launches a coroutine. shareIn(scope, started, replay) creates a MutableSharedFlow with that replay, an extra buffer that brings it up to at least 64 slots, and SUSPEND. Then it launches one coroutine in scope that collects the upstream into it. stateIn does the same with a MutableStateFlow(initialValue). Picture a building with one water pump (that coroutine) and a tap for every subscriber. started decides when the pump runs. Eagerly runs it from opening time, whether anyone is there. Lazily lets the first visitor switch it on, and nobody ever switches it off. WhileSubscribed(5_000) is a tap on a motion sensor that shuts the water off 5 s after the last person leaves.

Inside, WhileSubscribed watches subscriptionCount. When the count drops to 0, it waits stopTimeout and then sends STOP, which cancels the upstream collection. A subscriber who comes back first cancels that pending wait, so the pump never stopped. The figure shows an exact virtual-time run for an FX poller that emits run * 100 + i every second. Dashboard A leaves at 2.5 s and is back at 4 s: it gets 104, from the same run. A leaves again at 6 s, and STOP comes at 11 s. When A returns at 14 s, it gets the stale 111 first, and then 200 from run #2.

Three facts in that run catch people:

  • The upstream restarts from the top, because it is a cold flow collected again. Run #2 counts from 200, and a runningFold would start over.
  • The returning subscriber sees the stale value first. replayExpirationMillis = 0 resets the StateFlow to its initial value when the pump stops, so the late A gets -1 instead of 111.
  • With WhileSubscribed(), whose stop timeout is 0, every page reload is a STOP and a new START.
Java
// Java equivalent: connect with the first subscriber, disconnect 5 s after the last.
// After a disconnect Reactor reconnects with an empty replay cache, so no stale rate is shown.
Flux<Rate> live = feed.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
Kotlin
val live: StateFlow<Rate?> = feed.stateIn(
    appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), initialValue = null)

Reading .value is not a subscription. It is looking at the tap from the doorway, and it doesn't trip the sensor. A request cache built with Lazily or WhileSubscribed and read only through .value never starts: in the Try it, three requests at 3.5 s read [null, null, null], and the feed was fetched 0 times. With Eagerly they read the latest rate after 4 fetches.

Two more ways the pump goes wrong. If the upstream throws, the sharing coroutine dies and the exception goes to the scope's handler. Subscribers are not told. They stand at their taps and wait for ever, so put retry or retryWhen above shareIn. And shareIn inside a function that each request calls installs a new pump per call: 50 requests that each read one value left 50 sharing coroutines and 500 upstream polls after 10 s. Build the shared flow once, in a field, in a scope that you cancel when the service stops.

try.title: Watch the pump start, stop and restart
steps: Read SharingTimeline.kt. Before running it, write down when upstream START and STOP print, and what A gets each time it comes back.
Run it. Then run it with -Pargs=expire and with -Pargs=stop0, predicting each first.
Run the Java twin, the same script ten times faster on Reactor's replay(1).refCount. Compare the lines after A's second return.

code.title: SharingTimeline.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SharingStarted import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.stateIn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.StandardTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestCoroutineScheduler import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest // An FX poller shared with stateIn. Each run of the upstream is numbered and emits // run * 100 + i every 1,000 ms, so you can see when a run starts over. Virtual time. private class Poller(private val clock: TestCoroutineScheduler) { var starts = 0 @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) val flow: Flow<Int> = flow { val run = ++starts println(" t=${clock.currentTime}: upstream START #$run") try { var i = 0 while (true) { emit(run * 100 + i++); delay(1_000) } } finally { println(" t=${clock.currentTime}: upstream STOP #$run") } } } @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun dashboard(started: SharingStarted) = runTest { println("== $started, initialValue = -1") val poller = Poller(testScheduler) val rate: StateFlow<Int> = poller.flow.stateIn(backgroundScope, started, initialValue = -1) fun open() = backgroundScope.launch { rate.collect { println(" t=$currentTime: A got $it") } } var a = open() delay(2_500); a.cancel(); println(" t=$currentTime: A leaves") delay(1_500); println(" t=$currentTime: A comes back"); a = open() delay(2_000); a.cancel(); println(" t=$currentTime: A leaves") delay(8_000); println(" t=$currentTime: A comes back"); open() delay(1_500); println(" t=$currentTime: end, upstream starts=${poller.starts}") } // Request handlers that only read .value and never collect. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun readOnly() = runTest { println("== a cache that request handlers only read with .value") for (started in listOf(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SharingStarted.Lazily, SharingStarted.Eagerly)) { var fetches = 0 val feed = flow { while (true) { fetches++; emit("1.08${50 + fetches}"); delay(1_000) } } val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) val eurUsd: StateFlow<String?> = feed.stateIn(scope, started, initialValue = null) delay(3_500) println(" $started: three requests read ${List(3) { eurUsd.value }}, upstream fetches=$fetches") scope.cancel() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { when (args.firstOrNull()) { "expire" -> dashboard(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0)) "stop0" -> dashboard(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed()) else -> { dashboard(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)); readOnly() } } }

alt.title: SharingTimelineJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l07; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; // Java equivalent: Reactor's replay(1).refCount(1, grace), on the REAL clock. // Reactor's virtual clock lives in reactor-test, so this run is the Kotlin timeline // scaled down ten times: a rate every 100 ms and a 500 ms grace period. // Times vary by a few ms between runs. public class SharingTimelineJava { static long t0; static void log(String what) { if (t0 == 0) t0 = System.nanoTime(); // the clock starts at the first upstream START System.out.printf(" t=%4d ms: %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what); } static Disposable open(Flux<Integer> rate) { return rate.subscribe(v -> log("A got " + v)); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger starts = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<Integer> poller = Flux.defer(() -> { int run = starts.incrementAndGet(); log("upstream START #" + run); return Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofMillis(100)) .map(i -> run * 100 + i.intValue()) .doOnCancel(() -> log("upstream STOP #" + run)); }); Flux<Integer> rate = poller.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofMillis(500)); Disposable a = open(rate); Thread.sleep(250); a.dispose(); log("A leaves"); Thread.sleep(150); log("A comes back"); a = open(rate); Thread.sleep(200); a.dispose(); log("A leaves"); Thread.sleep(800); log("A comes back"); a = open(rate); Thread.sleep(150); a.dispose(); log("end, upstream starts=" + starts.get()); } }

try.expect: The default run: START #1 at 0, A gets 104 at 4000 with no restart, STOP #1 at 11000, and at 14000 A gets 111, then START #2 and 200, for 2 starts in all. In the .value part, WhileSubscribed and Lazily read [null, null, null] with 0 fetches, and Eagerly reads [1.0854, 1.0854, 1.0854] after 4 fetches. With expire, A gets -1 instead of 111 at 14000. With stop0, STOP #1 comes at 2500 and START #2 at 4000, where A gets the stale 102 and then 200; STOP #2 at 6000 and START #3 at 14000 make three starts. The Java twin keeps run #1 through the first return (A gets 104), stops about 500 ms after A leaves the second time, and on the late return prints START #2 and then 200 with no stale value, because Reactor's replay(1) begins a fresh cache for the new connection. Its times vary by a few ms.

analogy: A cold flow is a recording: everyone who presses play hears it from the start, on their own player. A hot flow is a radio station: one broadcast, and you hear whatever is on air when you tune in. A SharedFlow station records onto one tape loop that every listener's playback head reads, so the slowest listener decides when the tape is full. A StateFlow is a notice board with one sheet, and readers only look up when they have a moment. stateIn and shareIn are the building's water pump: Eagerly runs it from opening time, Lazily is switched on by the first visitor and never off, and WhileSubscribed is a motion sensor with a delay. The analogy breaks at the tape. A real radio station never waits for its slowest listener, and a SharedFlow with SUSPEND does exactly that.
world: In a payment service the hot shapes map onto different jobs. The FX rates that request handlers read through .value are a cache: stateIn(appScope, Eagerly, null) with a retry above it, as in the lab, because a cache that waits for a subscriber never fills. The live rates pushed to ops dashboards over server-sent events are a tap: WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), so a page reload keeps the provider connection and a dashboard opened at night never shows an old rate. Payment transitions that a notifier and an audit writer both consume are events: a MutableSharedFlow with a buffer, SUSPEND, a checked tryEmit from the Kafka listener thread, and a buffer of its own in front of the slow audit writer. And when a fraud handler and a ledger handler share one poll loop, the tape keeps nothing for a handler that subscribes late (with replay = 0): the records polled before it arrived are gone for it, unless the sharing waits for both, as in the worked example.
mistake: The most common mistake is a request cache copied from dashboard code: rates.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null), read in every handler with .value. Nothing ever collects it, and reading .value is not a subscription, so the feed never starts and every handler gets null. Lazily has the same trap. It passes a unit test that collects the flow to check it, which is the one thing the production code never does. Pick the strategy by who reads. Code that only reads .value needs Eagerly, or the suspend stateIn(scope) at start-up. Code that collects can use WhileSubscribed. Then put retry above stateIn, or the first feed error stops the cache for good while it keeps serving its last rate.

compare.title: One FX feed, shared for request handlers and for dashboards

java.title: FxRates.java (Reactor)
java.html: final class FxRates implements AutoCloseable { private final AtomicReference<Rate> latest = new AtomicReference<>(); private final Disposable cacheConnection; final Flux<Rate> live; FxRates(Flux<Rate> feed) { // for request handlers: connect now, retry after a second, keep the latest in a field this.cacheConnection = feed .retryWhen(Retry.fixedDelay(Long.MAX_VALUE, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException)) .subscribe(latest::set); // for dashboards: connect with the first, disconnect 5 s after the last this.live = feed.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } Rate current() { return latest.get(); } @Override public void close() { cacheConnection.dispose(); } }

kotlin.title: FxRates.kt (StateFlow)
kotlin.html: class FxRates(feed: Flow<Rate>, scope: CoroutineScope) { // for request handlers: .value is not a subscription, so start now val cache: StateFlow<Rate?> = feed .retry { e -> (e is IOException).also { if (it) delay(1_000) } } .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null) // for dashboards: survive a 5 s reload, then stop and forget the old rate val live: StateFlow<Rate?> = feed .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), null) fun current(): Rate? = cache.value } // cancelling `scope` stops both

compare.note: The Kotlin side needs no AtomicReference, because a StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it synchronously, and collectors get the same value with equality conflation built in. Lifetime differs too. Both Kotlin flows live in scope, so cancelling that one scope stops both upstream collections; in Reactor the cache lives as long as its Disposable, and the dashboard connection as long as it has subscribers. The two sides also forget differently. After a disconnect, replay(1).refCount reconnects with an empty cache, and Kotlin needs replayExpirationMillis = 0 for the same effect. Errors are where they differ most. In Reactor an error in the feed reaches every subscriber as onError. In Kotlin it ends the sharing coroutine, goes to the scope, and leaves the subscribers waiting, which is why the retry sits above stateIn. Both versions open two connections to the provider, one per view.

worked.title: Share one poll loop between a fraud handler and a ledger handler

steps.say: A service polls a Kafka-style source and hands every record to two handlers, fraud checks and ledger posting. Polling twice would read every record twice, so the poll loop is shared with shareIn and replay = 0. As their beans start, the fraud handler subscribes at 250 ms and the ledger handler at 500 ms. Predict what each has received by 800 ms.
steps.code: var offset = 0 val records = flow { while (true) { delay(100); emit("rec-${offset++}") } } // stands in for poll() val shared = records.shareIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly) // replay = 0 // fraud subscribes at t=250, ledger at t=500

alt.html: // Java equivalent: one connection, multicast to whoever is subscribed when a record arrives Flux<String> records = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).map(i -> "rec-" + i); Flux<String> shared = records.publish().autoConnect(0); // connect now, like Eagerly // fraud subscribes at t=250, ledger at t=500

steps.say: The virtual-time run. With Eagerly, rec-0 and rec-1 were polled before anyone listened, and the ledger handler also missed everything up to rec-4. WhileSubscribed() helps the first handler and not the second. With replay = 0 the tape keeps nothing for a late subscriber.
steps.code:
Eagerly:            fraud=[rec-2, rec-3, rec-4, rec-5, rec-6]  ledger=[rec-5, rec-6]
WhileSubscribed():  fraud=[rec-0, rec-1, rec-2, rec-3, rec-4]  ledger=[rec-2, rec-3, rec-4]

steps.say: Start the poll only when both handlers are there. SharingStarted is a fun interface that turns the subscriber count into START and STOP commands, so the gate is one line. In the same run, both handlers now get [rec-0, rec-1] by 800 ms.
steps.code: // 1. a strategy built on subscriptionCount val bothHandlers = SharingStarted { count -> count.map { if (it >= 2) SharingCommand.START else SharingCommand.STOP } } // 2. the same shareIn, gated val shared = records.shareIn(appScope, bothHandlers)

alt.html: // 1. and 2.: connect once two subscribers are there (Reactor's version never disconnects) Flux<String> shared = records.publish().autoConnect(2);

steps.say: Self-check: the ledger handler needs 50 ms per record and fraud needs 5 ms. With shareIn's default SUSPEND, which one sets the pace of the poll loop, and is that what you want here? (The ledger handler. The tape is full once the slowest handler has 64 records it hasn't taken, and then emit, the poll loop, waits. For records that must all be processed, that is the backpressure you want. A drop policy would lose records with no error.)

lab.title: Predict the tape, then share an FX feed two ways
steps: Run the tests. 24 of 25 fail: every SharedFlowRuleTest case and five of the six FxRatesTest cases.

In SharedFlowRule.kt, write predictTryEmits from the rule in the second section, without creating a flow. For each row, the test runs a real MutableSharedFlow and compares. Then write predictReceived.
In FxRates.kt, fix requestCache. Handlers only read .value, so pick the SharingStarted that doesn't wait for a subscriber, and add a retry above stateIn that waits 1,000 ms after an IOException.
Fix dashboardFeed: survive a reload within 5 s, stop 5 s after the last dashboard leaves, and reset to null when it stops.
Run the tests until all 25 pass. Then read how FxRatesTest counts feed starts and stops in virtual time, and why it never calls advanceUntilIdle().
hints: The rule has three cases: no subscribers, a drop policy, and SUSPEND. In the last one the answer depends only on the index of the call and replay + extraBufferCapacity.
predictReceived: SUSPEND and DROP_LATEST keep the first values that fit, and DROP_OLDEST keeps the last ones.
retry { e -> ... } takes a suspending predicate, so it can delay(1_000) before it returns true. It must sit before stateIn: once the sharing coroutine has died, nothing restarts it.
If the late-dashboard test sees the old rate first, you need the second parameter of WhileSubscribed.

drill.title: A transition bus, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class TransitionBus with fun publish(t: Transition): Boolean, called from a non-suspending Kafka listener callback, and val events: SharedFlow<Transition>. A burst of up to 64 transitions must not be refused, no transition may be dropped by a policy, and a slow audit subscriber must not hold back a fast notifier. Write the audit subscriber's collection too, and say in a comment when publish returns false.

answer.html: class TransitionBus { private val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Transition>(extraBufferCapacity = 64) // SUSPEND, the default val events: SharedFlow<Transition> = bus.asSharedFlow() // false only when some subscriber already has 64 transitions it hasn't taken; // the listener must not acknowledge the record then. With no subscriber it is // always true, and the transition goes nowhere. fun publish(t: Transition): Boolean = bus.tryEmit(t) } // the audit writer takes values off the shared buffer at once, into a channel of its own suspend fun auditAll(bus: TransitionBus, repo: AuditRepository) = bus.events.buffer(1_000).collect { repo.write(it) }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a buffered multicast sink, and a buffer of its own on the audit side class TransitionBus { private final Sinks.Many<Transition> bus = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); Flux<Transition> events() { return bus.asFlux(); } // false when the buffer is full (FAIL_OVERFLOW); synchronized because a Reactor sink // refuses concurrent emits with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED synchronized boolean publish(Transition t) { return bus.tryEmitNext(t).isSuccess(); } } Disposable auditAll(TransitionBus bus, AuditRepository repo) { return bus.events() .onBackpressureBuffer(1_000) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .subscribe(repo::write); }

recap: A MutableSharedFlow is one buffer of replay + extraBufferCapacity slots shared by every subscriber. It is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it hasn't taken, and a subscriber takes a value before its collect lambda runs.

When it is full, SUSPEND makes emit wait and tryEmit return false, DROP_LATEST drops the new value for everyone, and DROP_OLDEST makes only the slow subscriber skip. With no subscribers nothing ever waits.

The default MutableSharedFlow() has no buffer: a value passes like a relay baton, so tryEmit fails whenever anyone is subscribed, and emit returns once every subscriber has taken the value. A late subscriber gets the replay cache, then live values.

A StateFlow compares with equals when you set it and again in each collector. A busy collector sees only the latest value, so A, B, A while it is busy shows nothing. update { } may run its lambda many times.

shareIn and stateIn launch one coroutine in your scope. WhileSubscribed(5_000) survives a return within 5 s; after a stop the upstream restarts from the top, behind the stale value unless replayExpirationMillis = 0.

Reading .value is not a subscription, an upstream failure leaves subscribers waiting, and shareIn per call leaks a coroutine per call. Use Eagerly for caches, retry above the share, and one shared flow per service.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks two things: why did the fast notifier lose transitions under DROP_LATEST when only the audit writer was slow, and why does tryEmit on a default MutableSharedFlow() fail while the subscriber is idle? Answer both with the tape model, in a few sentences.
explain.answer: A MutableSharedFlow keeps one buffer of replay + extraBufferCapacity values, and every subscriber reads it at its own position. A value can only be cleared once the slowest subscriber has taken it, so the slowest subscriber decides when the buffer is full, for everyone. Under DROP_LATEST a value that finds the buffer full is never stored, so the fast notifier never sees it either. The default flow has no buffer at all. A value can only pass from an emit that is suspended and waiting to a subscriber that takes it, like a relay baton. tryEmit can't wait, so with any subscriber present it returns false, idle or not. With no subscriber it returns true, and the value goes nowhere.

deeper.html:
The internals, for a curious day. The field names here are private and may change in any release, so don't build on them.

Every collector of a shared flow gets a slot object from an array that starts at size 2 and doubles when full: 2 for one or two subscribers, 4 for three or four, 8 for five. A SharedFlow slot holds the index of the next value its collector will read, plus that collector's suspended continuation. The tape is a ring buffer, also allocated lazily and doubled when needed, and it holds the buffered values followed by the suspended emit calls as placeholder objects. Its start, head, is the smaller of the slowest collector's index and the start of the replay cache. When the slowest collector moves on, head moves, the old cells are cleared, and waiting emitters are resumed as their values move onto the tape. Every change happens under one lock, and the coroutines to resume are collected and resumed after the lock is released. The KDoc puts the cost of an emit at O(N) in the number of subscribers.

A StateFlow slot is one atomic field: free, waiting, pending, or a suspended continuation. An update marks every slot pending and copies nothing, which is why the KDoc calls StateFlow allocation-free. Concurrent updates use a sequence number that is odd while an update is being delivered. A second writer that arrives in the middle only bumps it, and the first writer loops round to deliver the newest value.

Two APIs in this area are experimental in 1.11.0 and need @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). resetReplayCache() empties the replay cache for new subscribers, while existing ones keep what they had; on a MutableStateFlow it throws UnsupportedOperationException: MutableStateFlow.resetReplayCache is not supported. SharedFlow.asFlow(), new in 1.11.0, hides the hot type from callers.

The suspend overload stateIn(scope) has no started. It launches the upstream in scope, suspends until the first value, and returns a StateFlow holding it: in one run, a config flow whose first value took 300 ms made stateIn return at t=300. That fits a config value loaded at start-up. An empty upstream throws NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty. An upstream that fails before its first value rethrows to the caller and also cancels the scope you passed, so choose that scope knowing it goes down with a failed load.

sources.title: Asynchronous Flow (Kotlin docs), including hot flows
